messages.subject: site abundance from predict() when assuming a zero inflated Poisson error structure and model pcount (N-Mixture)
messages.subject_clean: site abundance from predict() when assuming a zero inflated Poisson error structure and model pcount (N-Mixture)
messages.body_plain:
I have recently had a brief email exchange with Andy Royle about some
modeling I am doing using N-mixture models.  The question came up as
to whether the predict() function in umarked returned the mean
abundance in occupied sites (lambda) or the mean abundance weighted by
the occupancy rate (lambda*probability of site occupancy).  Andy
couldn't recall and suggested I write a simple model to see.  After I
did the work Andy suggested I post the results here for others to
see.  Hopefully it will benefit someone.

Hi Andy.  I did the simulation you suggested (code below).  I thought
you would like to know that It looks like predict() gives the lambda
unweighted by psi.  I also see that the interpretation of the psi
parameter in unmarked is a little tricky (see bottom of code).

Thanks again!

Lew

sites=1000
reps=20
int=2
slope=.025
truepsi=0.25
truedet=.3

x=(runif(sites,27,32))
state=rpois(sites,exp(int+slope*x))*rbinom(sites,1,truepsi)

obs=matrix(NA,sites,reps)
for(j in 1:reps){
  for(i in 1:sites){
  obs[i,j]=rbinom(1,state[i],truedet)
}
}
#obs

SCovs=data.frame(bottom=x)

counts=obs
n.mix.dat=unmarkedFramePCount(y=counts,siteCovs=SCovs)
mod=pcount(~1 ~bottom,data=n.mix.dat,K=25,mixture=c("ZIP"),engine="C")

backTransform(mod,'det')
coef(mod)

x2=seq(27,32,length.out=20)
eststate=predict(mod,'state',data.frame(bottom=x2))

plot(x,state)
lines(x2,eststate[,1])
lines(x2,exp(int+slope*seq(27,32,length.out=20)),col='blue')

#true psi is:
truepsi

#this is expit of estimated psi:
1/(1+exp(-coef(mod)[4]))

#this is 1- expit of estimated psi (complement):
1-1/(1+exp(-coef(mod)[4]))

#THIS MUST BE WHY IT IS CALLED "Zero Inflation" in the model
summary..... BUT NAMING THE PARAMETER "psi" IS CONFUSING

I’ve also been doing some simulations with pcount and zip, based on the simulation presented with the pcount function in the unmarked 0.9-7 manual manual (p. 48).  Unlike the predict function, it appears that the empirical Bayes function ‘ranef’ gives estimates that are the mean (or mode) abundance weighted by occupancy for zip models.  I’ve noticed that when p(detection) is reasonably high (say 0.5, as in scenario 1 of my script), pcount with zip does a good job of modeling the zip data.  When p(detection) is low (say 0.1, as in scenario 2 of my script), it doesn’t necessarily do so well.  This is understandable because when p(detection) is low, it must be difficult to differentiate between unoccupied sites and occupied sites that happened never to produce a detection.  The latter situation seems to apply to a real data set that I’m dealing with on clapper rails.  I’m inclined to go with the basic Poisson model for the rails rather than the zip (even though the zip is superior by the usual model comparison criteria) because the basic Poisson seems at worst to give somewhat of an underestimate of overall abundance, whereas the zip potentially gives a large overestimate when p(detection) is low.  I suppose that I could also do an occupancy model in conjunction with the basic Poisson model to get a handle on site occupancy rate.

My simulation script is below. Any comments (including on my thoughts on using the basic Poisson for the rails) or corrections are welcome.  BTW using ‘mean(bup(ranef …’ in the script may be arguable when the bups aren’t normally distributed but median or mode didn’t seem to work obviously better.

RK

library(unmarked)

# Simulate data

# scenario 1:  true detection p = 0.5

# scenario 2: true detection p = 0.1

set.seed(27) #This seed produces data that exemplify the issue with low p(detect);

                      #results with other seeds may differ.

nSites <- 1000

nVisits <- 3

lambda <- 3

psi <- 0.33

# p <- 0.50    #scenario 1 good result

  p <- 0.10    #scenario 2 not so good result

N <- rpois(nSites, lambda) # latent abundance

y <- matrix(NA, nSites, nVisits)

for(j in 1:nVisits) y[,j] <- rbinom(nSites, N, p)

for(i in 1:nSites) if(runif(1,0,1)<psi) y[i,1:3] <- 0

umf <- unmarkedFramePCount(y=y)

summary(umf)

# Fit a ZIP model

fmZIP <- pcount(~1 ~1, umf, mixture="ZIP", K=100)

summary(fmZIP)

(plogis(coef(fmZIP, type="det")))# Should be close to p

(plogis(confint(fmZIP,type="det")))

(plogis(coef(fmZIP, type="psi"))) # Should be close to psi

(plogis(confint(fmZIP, type="psi")))

(exp(coef(fmZIP,type="state")))  # Should be close to lambda

(exp(confint(fmZIP,type="state")))

#2 ways to estimate overall mean abundance:

(exp(coef(fmZIP,type="state")))*(1-(plogis(coef(fmZIP, type="psi"))))

(mean(bup(ranef(fmZIP))))

colMeans(confint(ranef(fmZIP)))

hist(bup(ranef(fmZIP)))

# Fit a basic Poisson model

fmPois <- pcount(~1 ~1, umf, mixture="P", K=100)

summary(fmPois)

(plogis(coef(fmPois, type="det")))

(plogis(confint(fmPois,type="det"))) #

(exp(coef(fmPois,type="state")))

(exp(confint(fmPois,type="state")))

mean(bup(ranef(fmPois)))

colMeans(confint(ranef(fmPois)))

messages.subject_clean: ranef() vs. predict() for colext models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Richard, Andy, et al.

Can someone enlighten me to the differences between outputs of predict() and ranef() for colext models?

I've seen it referenced several times here and, in reading the manual (but not too far into the sources cited), I do like the idea of obtaining estimates of the latent occupancy state of sites in which a species was not detected.

I've been comparing site-specific estimates of psi from a two-season model and my initial impression was that the ranef() distributions are driven solely by the detection part of the colext model.  This agrees with what I think of as the latent occupancy state of a site: observable when detected at least once but not when undetected (though estimable).

Two observations gave me this impression:
1) if a site was ever occupied it had a value of 1 using ranef() vs. a high probability (e.g. 0.8) using predict()
2) if observations were "forced" to all 0s (never detected) or 1s (detected >= once) and the pformula of the model set to a constant (pformula=~1), ranef() produced values of only 1 or 0 (or ever, ever so slightly larger than 0)

However, using real data as in observation 1, I've  tried adjusting covariates (or omitting them altogether) in other parts of the model (e.g. psi, gamma, epsilon) while keeping the pformula the same and the ranef() results will vary (though still producing 1s for sites with >= 1 detection), so probabilities are dependent on other parts of the model (as indicated in the manual; Pr(N=k|y,psi,gamma,epsilon,p).  I just don't understand how (and, to be honest, why) the latent state is dependent on anything other than y and p.

I'd like to use these posterior distributions from ranef() when appropriate, I just want to be sure when is most appropriate.

My deepest gratitude for your continued development of the unmarked package and for maintaining this group!

Giancarlo

messages.body_plain:
Dear Giancarlo,

Take a look at the algebra of the model. The occupancy model you're fitting is the following (I write the single-season model, because the issue applies equally in single-season and multi-seasons; also, I drop indices):

1. z ~ Bernoulli(psi)
2. y ~ Bernoulli(z * p)

Eq. 1 is the description of the latent occupancy state (z) as a function of the occcupancy parameter (psi), and eq. 2 is the description of the relationship between the observed detection/nondetection datum (y) and the latent state (z) and detection probability (p).

Now here's the essential difference between predict() and ranef():
predict() gives you an estimate of psi for each site, while ranef() gives you an estimate of z for each site (z_hat; hat for "estimate"). psi_hat is the expected probability for a site to be occupied, given any site covariates. z_hat is your best guess at the occupancy state ("occupied" or "not occupied"), given the observed data (y), the expected occupancy (psi_hat), detection probability and the number of surveys made at that site.

Hence, whenever y=1 for one of the reps at a site, z_hat is equal to one. AND, if your model is a good one, it will also yield a high occupancy probability for that site.

In contrast, whenever a species was never observed at a site (i.e., all y=0), then z_hat will be higher (a) when the expected occupancy probability for that site is higher, (b) when p for that site is lower and (c) when there are fewer rep surveys.

All this can be put in algebra, but this is an attempt to describe things (mostly) in words.

Kind regards  -  Marc

Can someone enlighten me to the differences between outputs of predict() and ranef() for colext models?

I've seen it referenced several times here and, in reading the manual (but not too far into the sources cited), I do like the idea of obtaining estimates of the latent occupancy state of sites in which a species was not detected.

However, using real data as in observation 1, I've  tried adjusting covariates (or omitting them altogether) in other parts of the model (e.g. psi, gamma, epsilon) while keeping the pformula the same and the ranef() results will vary (though still producing 1s for sites with >= 1 detection), so probabilities are dependent on other parts of the model (as indicated in the manual; Pr(N=k|y,psi,gamma,epsilon,p).  I just don't understand how (and, to be honest, why) the latent state is dependent on anything other than y and p.

I'd like to use these posterior distributions from ranef() when appropriate, I just want to be sure when is most appropriate.

My deepest gratitude for your continued development of the unmarked package and for maintaining this group!

Giancarlo

messages.body_plain:
Aude,

The problem with your current model is that date is not a
site-specific attribute, while psi is trying to estimate a site-specific
 probability (if there are covariates).  You could model detection as
varying with date (p~date) if you think the detectability of
reproduction changes with date.  But I'm not sure how date would affect
the probability of reproduction at a site.

I would consider using
 a multi-state model.  It sounds like you have
data for sites where the species was not observed.  So you should be
able to model the probability of presence and the probability of
reproduction, conditional on presence (sensu Nichols et al. 2007
Ecology).  Date could then potentially affect your
probability of detecting reproduction (delta in the Nichols paper).  If
you are content with simply modeling the probability of reproduction
given observed
presence (using only those sites with observed presence), then at a
least an occupancy
model will allow an estimate of detection probability.  But you've
conditioned your inference on sites where the species was observed, and
obviously observed presence does not always equal presence.

Like
Marc said, if you are interested in estimating nest success then you
should consider looking into models of daily survival rate (Dinsmore et
al. 2002 and Stanley 2004).  Those models typically require more
frequent visitations than occupancy models, if you want your survival
estimates to have any precision.

-Dan

Hi Pablo,

The latent variable is N(i), the abundance at site i. An estimator of abundance in the sampled area, N, is the sum of the estimates of N(i). Here's an example for computing this, based on the example for occuRN:

data(birds)
woodthrushUMF <- unmarkedFrameOccu(woodthrush.bin)
(fm.wood.rn <- occuRN(~ 1 ~ 1, woodthrushUMF, K=25))
# Empirical Bayes estimates of abundance at each site
re <- ranef(fm.wood.rn, K=25)
plot(re)
Ni.hat <- bup(re, "mode")
N.hat <- sum(Ni.hat)

Richard
